item.title: The 'developed country' label is actually a trap: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 00:30:00
A busy scene at the Port of Shanghai on July 24, 2026 Photo: VCG The international discussions on the positioning of China's development are an acknowledgment of China's developmental achievements and its responsibilities as a major power. However, we must be vigilant against certain narratives that deliberately obscure China's developmental stage, impose obligations that exceed its current phase of development, constrict China's developmental space, and create rifts between China and other developing countries, therefore putting China in a difficult position. The Wall Street Journal recently published an article saying that China is on the cusp of becoming a high-income country by the World Bank's classification. "China doesn't want to join the ranks of the world's developed countries," the article claimed, arguing that China benefits from its current status in international groups as "developing." In fact, being a high-income country is not the same as being a developed country. By conflating the two concepts, the Wall Street Journal article attempts to exert public pressure on China to shoulder international obligations that go beyond its current level of development. According to World Bank estimates, China's gross national income (GNI) per capita stood at $14,230 in 2025, slightly below the high-income threshold of $14,375. It is worth noting that this World Bank classification is based solely on GNI per capita, rather than a comprehensive assessment of a country's level of modernization, industrial development and public services. In recent years, countries such as Chile, Uruguay, Panama and Costa Rica have crossed the World Bank's high-income threshold. However, they are still widely regarded by the international community as developing countries or emerging economies, rather than automatically being classified as developed countries simply because they have reached the high-income threshold. As Chinese modernization steadily advances, China has made historic achievements in economic and social development, with its GDP firmly ranking second in the world. However, multiple indicators show that China's status as a developing country remains unchanged. For example, there is still a significant gap in per capita GDP compared to developed economies like those in Europe and the US, regional development imbalances have not yet been fundamentally resolved, and disparities persist between urban and rural areas. By contrast, the development process of Western developed countries is a comprehensive state formed after highly mature industrialization, urbanization, and modernization. This is reflected not only in the scale of their economies but also in various dimensions such as per capita wealth, social security systems, public service capacity, and scientific and technological innovation systems. The international discussions on the positioning of China's development largely stem from the rapid pace of China's growth and its significant contributions to the global economy, which have long surpassed the conventional narrative framework for traditional developing countries. These discussions are an acknowledgment of China's developmental achievements and its responsibilities as a major power. However, we must be vigilant against certain narratives that deliberately obscure China's developmental stage, impose obligations that exceed its current phase of development, constrict China's developmental space, and create rifts between China and other developing countries, therefore putting China in a difficult position. For China, its status as a developing country carries special political significance. China has always been a member of the Global South. This "South" is not merely a geographical or economic concept but an identity formed by emerging market countries and developing nations based on similar historical circumstances, current stages of development, common developmental goals, and shared political aspirations. Those who are eager to label China as a "developed country" are not truly seeking China's "graduation," but rather its "exclusion," aiming to detach China from the Global South camp. In this regard, China is very clear-minded and will not fall into this trap. To assess a country's international responsibilities, one should not only consider whether it has been labeled a "developed country," but rather whether it is genuinely promoting global common development. China's average annual contribution to global economic growth has long been around 30 percent. China is the largest contributor of peacekeeping personnel among the permanent members of the UN Security Council, and its four global initiatives offer Chinese wisdom,solutions and strength for global governance. China's contributions to building an open, inclusive, clean and beautiful world that enjoys lasting peace, common security, and common prosperity have already surpassed those of many developed countries. However, China will always be a member of the developing world; this is not modesty, but a reflection of sobriety and a sense of responsibility.

item.title: Xi calls for decisive progress in Healthy China advancement
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-14 00:11:00
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, delivers an important speech during a national meeting on health in Beijing. The meeting was held in Beijing on October 12 and 13, 2026. Photo: Xinhua Chinese President Xi Jinping has called for efforts to firmly follow a path with Chinese characteristics in developing the country's health programs, to secure decisive progress in the Healthy China Initiative over the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030). Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks at a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday, according to the Xinhua News Agency. Xi stressed that people's health is a key benchmark of a nation's prosperity and strength. The meeting comes as China begins implementing its national health plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period, which sets out a roadmap for improving healthcare accessibility, strengthening disease prevention and accelerating medical innovation over the next five years. Under the plan released by the State Council in July, China aims to raise its average life expectancy to 80 years by 2030, from 79.25 years in 2025, while bringing its major health indicators in line with those of high-income economies. The plan also underlines major tasks to optimize all-round life-cycle health services for all people, shore up robust health safeguards, build an integrated, high-quality medical network, cultivate new growth engines for the health sector, and advance health-centered governance in the sector. Since the 18th CPC National Congress in 2012, the Party has made a major decision to launch the Healthy China Initiative, promoting the establishment of the world's largest systems of medical services, traditional medicine, disease prevention and control, and healthcare security, said Xi, noting that the country has achieved historic accomplishments and made all-round progress in healthcare. He said the goal is to build a Healthy China, where health services are ensured in a balanced, inclusive, high-quality and efficient manner. Prevention, he said, is the most cost-effective and efficient approach to protecting public health. He called for greater emphasis on foundational health work, addressing risks at their source, and encouraging the public to adopt a sound understanding of health and take an active role in managing their own well-being. The emphasis on prevention reflects a shift in China's approach to public health, from treating diseases after they occur toward addressing health risks at their source and promoting well-being across society, medical and health policy professionals noted. Cui Xiaobo, a professor at the School of Public Health, Capital Medical University, told the Global Times that putting prevention first means moving the focus of healthcare further upstream, reducing health risks before diseases develop rather than relying primarily on treatment after illness occurs. Looking ahead, Cui said a key priority should be making healthcare services more equitable and accessible by strengthening primary healthcare, improving the distribution of medical resources and building a stable medical workforce, particularly in rural and underserved areas. These priorities are also central to China's efforts to translate its long-term Healthy China 2035 vision into concrete improvements during the next five years. Zeng Guang, former chief epidemiologist with the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, told the Global Times that the 15th Five-Year Plan period will be crucial for strengthening China's healthcare system. "Whenever new public health challenges emerge, we must be able to respond effectively," Zeng said, stressing the importance of addressing weaknesses and building a more resilient healthcare system. Beyond improving access to healthcare, Zeng pointed to the potential of artificial intelligence and smart healthcare technologies to enhance medical diagnosis and healthcare delivery. Health beyond borders Efforts will also be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, work with other countries to address major challenges in the health sector, and continuously improve the health and well-being of people around the world, Xi said. Such international engagement has been reflected in more than six decades of Chinese medical teams working in other developing countries, particularly across Africa, where Chinese doctors have provided treatment, shared medical expertise and helped train local healthcare professionals. Since China dispatched its first overseas medical team to Algeria in 1963, approximately 30,000 Chinese medical workers have served in 76 countries and regions, treating around 290 million patients, according to Xinhua figures published in August. China's medical cooperation is increasingly focused on leaving behind lasting capabilities rather than providing treatment alone. Since 1963, Chinese medical teams have trained more than 100,000 local healthcare workers, while Chinese and African hospitals have developed partnerships and jointly established specialized medical centers. Beyond providing medical treatment, China's overseas medical assistance has increasingly focused on helping developing countries build their own healthcare capacity, particularly through technology transfer and the training of local medical professionals. Sun Hui, a member of China's third medical team dispatched to Kiribati, told the Global Times on Tuesday that one of the most significant changes in more than six decades of China's overseas medical assistance has been the shift from treating patients to cultivating local medical expertise. During his assignment at Tungaru Central Hospital in Kiribati, Sun found that the lack of gastrointestinal endoscopy equipment made it difficult to diagnose many digestive diseases. To address the challenge, the Chinese medical team introduced gastrointestinal contrast-enhanced ultrasound techniques, helping local doctors diagnose conditions including tumors and biliary tract abnormalities. More importantly, the team provided hands-on training to local ultrasound technicians, enabling them to apply the technology independently. The Chinese doctors also conducted medical outreach visits to outer islands and offered remote guidance on clinical cases. The efforts have continued with subsequent Chinese medical teams. China's fifth medical team arrived in Tarawa, Kiribati, in December 2025. As of August 19, 2026, the team had handled 3,150 outpatient and emergency visits, treated 1,650 inpatients, performed 756 surgeries and administered anesthesia in 850 cases, the Global Times learned from the fifth team on Tuesday. Beyond hospital-based treatment, the team conducted six medical outreach missions to outer islands, providing much-needed healthcare services to more than 2,000 residents. It also organized or participated in nine free medical clinics in Tarawa, extending healthcare services to more local communities, the team revealed. "We hope to take home only our luggage while leaving behind medical expertise, and to take home memories while leaving behind a medical team capable of continuing to serve the local people," Su Bing, a member of the fifth Chinese medical team said. In the Solomon Islands, the China-aided Comprehensive Medical Center at the National Referral Hospital in Honiara opened in June 2025, providing facilities for specialist care and clinical training. Chu Liangzhao, head of the fifth Chinese medical team to the country, told the Global Times that his team had added neurosurgery and breast surgery to its specialties after taking over in March 2026. Chinese and local doctors work together in consultations, operations and ward rounds, combining patient care with practical training. Internationally, the five-year health plan released in July also calls for establishing health cooperation hubs based at leading domestic hospitals to advance global collaboration in clinical research, the application of cutting-edge medical technologies and international healthcare services. It also underscores the need to deepen health cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative, while expanding overseas medical assistance in areas such as public health and traditional medicine. Chen Hong, director of the Asia Pacific Studies Center at East China Normal University, told the Global Times that China's medical cooperation with Pacific island countries is designed to address their practical healthcare needs, rather than simply provide short-term assistance. "For people in these island countries, China's friendship is not an abstract diplomatic commitment. It is reflected in their ability to receive medical treatment, undergo surgery and have their lives saved," Chen said. More broadly, Chen said China's efforts to share medical technologies, resources and development experience reflect its commitment to promoting a more equitable and inclusive global public health system.

item.title: Chinese top diplomat meets UAE president's special envoy Khaldoon
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 22:53:00
China UAE Chinese top diplomat Wang Yi met with Khaldoon Khalifa Al Mubarak, special envoy of the UAE president for China affairs, in Beijing on Tuesday, with the two sides discussing bilateral ties and the evolving situation in the Middle East, as experts said the visit reflects the UAE's expectations for China to play a greater role in promoting regional de-escalation and advancing practical cooperation. Wang, a member of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and director of the Office of the Central Commission for Foreign Affairs, said China and the UAE enjoy strong political mutual trust and have achieved substantive results in cooperation. Their relationship has gone beyond the bilateral scope and become a model of cooperation among Global South countries in pursuing development and revitalization, Wang said. Regardless of changes in the international and regional situation, China is ready to work with the UAE under the guidance of the two countries' heads of state to take bilateral relations to new heights, Wang said. Peace cannot be achieved easily, and efforts to promote reconciliation and end conflicts require collective action, Wang said, expressing China's belief that a brighter future for the region can be achieved if all parties remain committed to peace. China will continue to contribute to regional peace and stability by promoting a comprehensive ceasefire, advancing political solutions, facilitating the early resumption of negotiations and working toward lasting peace, Wang said. Khaldoon congratulated China on the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. He also thanked China for its warm reception of UAE Crown Prince Khaled during his visit to China and expressed expectations for a meeting between the two countries' leaders within the year. Khaldoon briefed Wang on the situation in the Gulf and the broader Middle East, as well as the UAE's efforts, and said his country is willing to strengthen communication and coordination with China to jointly promote regional peace and stability. China is a trusted and reliable partner of the UAE, Khaldoon said, expressing the hope that bilateral comprehensive strategic partnership would reach new heights. Against the backdrop of declining US willingness to resolve Middle East issues, the UAE as a major regional shipping hub has greater reason to seek diplomatic coordination with China, Sun Degang, director of the Center for Middle Eastern Studies at Fudan University, said. The visit signals higher expectations for Beijing's role in addressing regional issues, easing tensions and helping stabilize the situation, he noted. The frequent high-level exchanges between China and Arab countries this year reflect the importance regional states attach to China's role, Sun said. A potential visit by the UAE president to China would further strengthen cooperation among Global South countries, particularly given the UAE's leading position in high technology in the Arab world, he added. Sun said there is potential room for China and the UAE to expand cooperation in energy, new energy, artificial intelligence and other high-tech sectors. Such a shift would allow China to better combine its technological strengths with the UAE's capital advantages, creating new opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation, Sun noted. Ding Long, a professor at the Middle East Studies Institute of Shanghai International Studies University, said the envoy's visit serves three main purposes: laying the groundwork for a potential visit by the UAE president and preparing the agenda for high-level talks, exchanging views on the increasingly complex and escalating Middle East situation, and advancing the implementation of bilateral cooperation projects. The UAE president has made few overseas visits since the outbreak of the latest round in the regional conflict, making a potential trip to China particularly significant in demonstrating the importance Abu Dhabi attaches to bilateral ties, Ding said. The substantial results and frequent communication between the two sides demonstrate that practical cooperation and diplomatic coordination can continue even amid a complex international environment, he added.

item.title: Chinese doctors help save a child's kidneys and train local surgeons in growing medical partnership with PNG
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 22:33:00
Chinese and Papua New Guinean doctors perform surgery to remove a tumor at Port Moresby General Hospital in Papua New Guinea on August 24, 2026. Photos on this page: Courtesy of Chinese medical team in PNG "I won the 'China in My Eyes' competition, hosted by the Chinese Embassy!" Papua New Guinean doctor Mazel Kerry Ipakasa wrote in a recent post on his LinkedIn account. His winning entry was a video documenting the medical partnership between China and Papua New Guinea (PNG), a collaboration he had experienced firsthand. "As a residential dental surgeon at Port Moresby General Hospital, I have had the privilege of working alongside the 15th China Medical Team," he said. Through footage of joint operations and everyday exchanges, Ipakasa shared how Chinese specialists treated patients and mentored local colleagues, including his own experience learning microvascular surgical techniques. For Xu Wei, captain of the 15th Chinese medical team to PNG, the video came as both a surprise and a gift. "The local doctors came up with the idea to make the video. We were deeply moved when we saw it," Xu told the Global Times. Receiving recognition from the people they worked with and served meant a great deal to the team, he said. The partnership captured in the video is part of China's broader efforts to strengthen international medical cooperation. At a national meeting on health held in Beijing on Monday and Tuesday, China called for efforts to be made to actively promote the building of a global community of health for all, according to the Xinhua News Agency. China has sent medical aid teams to 59 countries and regions since late 2012. Beyond treating patients, Chinese medical teams have also worked with local counterparts to share expertise and improve healthcare services. In PNG, such cooperation has continued for more than two decades. Ipakasa's video also comes as the two countries mark the 50th anniversary of diplomatic relations this year. China began dispatching medical teams to PNG in 2002, with the latest team working alongside local doctors at Port Moresby General Hospital. Behind the partnership captured on camera lies an ongoing task: adapting medical technology to local conditions and helping PNG doctors acquire the skills to use it themselves. Making technology work Seven-year-old Grace arrived at Port Moresby General Hospital with pain and fever in late March. She would undergo the last of three operations in August. Stones had formed in both her kidneys, blocking the flow of urine and causing a serious infection. Without effective treatment, both kidneys risked lasting damage, according to a case report provided by the Chinese medical team. Chinese urologist Zhang Teng and his local colleagues planned to treat her in stages. They needed to remove the stones while bringing the infection under control. But controlling the infection proved difficult. Even after weeks of treatment, the infection persisted. A drainage tube accidentally came out, adding another setback. Then the laser equipment that was needed to break up the stones stopped working. Zhang contacted an engineer in China. Through a video connection, they worked together to identify the fault and repair the equipment. One more difficulty remained: the hospital lacked a child-sized instrument needed to reach the remaining stone in her ureter, the tube carrying urine from the kidney to the bladder. Zhang combined the instruments available, reaching the stone through a small opening into the kidney. According to the team's case report, the approach helped preserve her kidney function and avoid injury to the ureter. On August 19, he completed the last of three operations. Nearly five months after treatment began, the team reported that Grace was recovering well and both her kidneys had been preserved. The medical challenges had been complex. The goal throughout was something any family could understand: helping a 7-year-old child recover while protecting her health for the years ahead. A Chinese doctor talks to a child in Papua New Guinea. Such cases demand adjustments that go beyond choosing a surgical technique. Xu told the Global Times that treatment plans that are familiar and routine in China cannot always be carried out as expected in PNG. Complex cases sometimes require remote consultations with specialists at the hospitals supporting the mission, the Global Times learned from the medic team. The current team comprises 10 members: eight medical specialists, an interpreter and a cook. Organized by Chongqing University Cancer Hospital, it draws doctors from several hospitals across Southwest China's Chongqing Municipality. The specialists work as consultants alongside local colleagues in fields including cardiology, surgery, newborn medicine, gynecology and traditional Chinese medicine. By August 31, the team had participated in or led 588 operations and introduced more than 80 new techniques and projects, according to the team's work summary. More than 100 medical professionals applied for the eight specialist positions, Xu told the Global Times. The roughly year-long assignment began in October 2025. Members completed individual handovers with their predecessors from the 14th team, helping maintain continuity in clinical work and training between successive postings. At first, Xu's decision to take the assignment began with a sense of responsibility. "Representing our country on a medical aid mission is a great honor," he told the Global Times. Working in PNG gave that responsibility a direct, personal meaning. Through treatment, he said, doctors could help local people experience the benefits of cooperation in their own lives. The experience also deepened his appreciation for the stable environment and healthcare support available at home. That backing extends into the team's daily work abroad, through specialist advice, equipment and supplies from China. "I am grateful to our country, which is always quietly supporting us," Xu said. Let local doctors take the lead An operation becomes a teaching opportunity when a local colleague takes the lead and the visiting specialist guides each step - Xu describes this as a central responsibility of the medical team. "What matters more than performing the operations ourselves is teaching local doctors how to perform them," he told the Global Times. Teaching continues during surgery, as Chinese specialists explain procedures and help colleagues develop the skills to carry them out. At Port Moresby General Hospital, that process is changing how pacemaker procedures are performed. Before the current team's arrival, the hospital conducted approximately three to four pacemaker implantations a year, with electrodes placed at the tip of the right ventricle, the Global Times learned from the team. Chinese cardiologist Zhang Xiaoliang introduced additional implantation techniques, including left bundle branch area pacing. This approach places an electrode near the heart's natural electrical conduction system, helping coordinate the contractions that pump blood. Introducing the procedure required preparation across several stages of care. The team reviewed the steps from preoperative assessment to electrode placement and postoperative adjustments, while providing training and surgical demonstrations, according to its account of the procedure. During one operation documented by the team, a local lead surgeon carried out the vein puncture, guided the wire and implanted the electrode under the Chinese specialist's guidance. Imaging helped locate the target area, and subsequent testing confirmed that the pacing parameters met the required standards. Local doctors Wesong Boko and Noah Tapaua completed structured training in the technique. Of five left bundle branch area pacing procedures reported by the team, Tapaua led three. The other two were conducted as teaching cases. Those procedures formed part of 20 pacemaker implantations completed during the current team's posting, according to its work summary. The collaboration also produced a jointly developed operating manual and a care pathway covering patient screening, surgery and follow-up. These give the local team a shared reference for decisions before and after implantation. Training extended to the staff supporting the procedures. On August 7, Zhang held a practical course on cardiac anatomy and pacing, bringing together cardiologists, catheterization laboratory nurses and other medical personnel. Participants identified structures in anatomical specimens, practiced locating implantation sites and reviewed clinical cases. The course connected the anatomy underlying the technique with the decisions required during an actual operation. A similar progression is taking place in chest surgery. Xu, a thoracic surgeon, said he teaches local colleagues while performing minimally invasive procedures. His aim is to help them develop the ability to carry out the surgery without needing him at the operating table. Xu acknowledged that participation varies. Some colleagues actively seek new knowledge and pursue further training in China; others are more inclined to leave complex procedures to the Chinese specialists while they remain available. By August 31, the Chinese team had conducted 152 teaching and training sessions, according to its work summary. Members of the Chinese medical team provide health checks, hygiene education and donate supplies for 45 children at the Life PNG Care center in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea, on November 17, 2025. Lasting and sustainable efforts Over the past 50 years, the friendship between China and PNG, transcending mountains and seas, has withstood the test of time and become a cherished asset for both peoples. Medical cooperation also features in celebrations marking 50 years of China-PNG diplomatic relations. In an anniversary article published on October 12, Chinese Ambassador to PNG Yang Xiaoguang noted that China had sent medical teams to PNG for 24 consecutive years and arranged three hospital ship visits. By December 2025, China had dispatched 15 teams involving 149 medical personnel to PNG, Xinhua reported. Meanwhile, Xu and his colleagues are exploring broader ways to make this medical partnership more sustainable and ensure its benefits last. The team has been visiting schools and workplaces. At Butuka Academy in February, doctors provided free consultations and taught students about oral health. At Goodman Fielder International in May, 101 employees received health checks and practical training in cardiopulmonary resuscitation. Most had never previously had a comprehensive health check, according to the team's records. Medical knowledge reaches newspaper readers, too. In November 2025, the team launched a regular health column in the Post-Courier, a leading local newspaper. Its first installment, written by urologist Zhang Teng, explained prostate problems in everyday language, including warning signs, screening and when to seek help, the Chongqing News reported. Designed as a monthly series drawing on different specialists' expertise, the column extends health education to people the doctors may never meet. Training brings colleagues together in more organized settings. More than 30 local health workers attended an August 6 workshop at Port Moresby General Hospital, which also hosted a surgical skills competition. At the University of Papua New Guinea's School of Medicine and Health Sciences, the team delivered clinical courses across eight specialties. Teaching materials and a collection of clinical cases were handed over for continued use by local teachers, the Global Times learned from the team. The cooperation has also extended to hospital construction outside the capital. In June 2022, a Chinese-supported provincial hospital in Enga was handed over to the PNG government. At the ceremony in Engan capital of Wabag, Prime Minister James Marape thanked China for supporting the project and expressed interest in deepening cooperation between the two countries, Xinhua reported. Back in Port Moresby, exchanges also extend to the Chinese-language classroom. More than 130 hospital employees and university students completed 24 weeks of lessons taught by the team's interpreter, Niu Tengfei, with songs and paper cutting accompanying everyday conversation, according to the team's work summary. Recognition from the people they worked with and served mattered deeply to the team, Xu said. Ipakasa's video offered one such response. "It is a legacy we will pass down to the next generation of doctors," Ipakasa said in the video.

item.title: GT Voice: What Paris Motor Show signals about China-Europe auto co-op
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 22:09:00
The Paris Motor Show runs October 12-18, 2026 in Paris, France. Photo: VCG The biennial Paris Motor Show officially kicked off on Monday, with a record number of Chinese automakers taking part to showcase their latest models and technologies. A total of 25 Chinese brands, represented by 16 companies, including BYD, XPeng, Changan, Dongfeng and Leapmotor, are taking part, roughly double the number at the 2024 edition. Such a scale of participation from Chinese carmakers would have been almost unimaginable a decade ago, yet it is now very much a real scene in the exhibition halls of the Paris Motor Show. Behind this lies the rapid rise of Chinese automakers globally. The Paris show has long served as a reliable barometer of the global auto industry, and this year's edition sent an unmistakable signal: China-Europe electric vehicle (EV) cooperation is moving from simple trade to deeper industrial integration. Compared with the previous show, Chinese brands' recognition, user base and market foothold in Europe have grown noticeably, and their development path has gradually shifted from pure vehicle exports toward deep localization, with production bases, research and development (R&D) centers, distribution networks and after-sales systems being established across Europe. For a long time, some in Europe have viewed Chinese carmakers through a zero-sum lens, framing normal market competition as a "shock" to local industries. This year's Paris Motor Show, however, makes clear that framing such cooperation simply as a threat no longer holds against the increasingly diverse and pragmatic reality in China-Europe cooperation. Chinese carmakers are using flexible approaches such as joint plant construction and joint development to revitalize existing local capacity, drive employment and supply chains, and offer European consumers more cost-effective models. This model is not zero-sum but complementary. For instance, Stellantis and China's Leapmotor announced plans in May to start joint car production in Europe, with two models to be built in Spain, deepening their tie-up beyond distribution into manufacturing. This is a win-win arrangement, as European companies need such cooperation to raise productivity, while Chinese automakers need a localized foundation to take root in the market. Europe's vehicle industry stands at a critical stage of electrification, and Chinese carmakers' strengths in batteries, electronic controls and intelligent systems align neatly with Europe's robust manufacturing base and brand heritage. Joint plants shorten construction cycles and reduce policy risk, while joint development shares R&D costs and speeds up product iteration. This is not one side swallowing the other, but making the cake bigger together. An increasing number of European industry bodies, local partners and ordinary consumers are recognizing the real value of this cooperation. The jobs created, technology spillovers and industrial increments brought by Chinese brands cannot be overlooked. For example, BYD plans to expand its European workforce to more than 40,000 people by 2030, a target that would place the Chinese carmaker among the largest non-European automotive employers in the region, according to Bloomberg. This tangible market dividend is far more persuasive than any protectionist slogan. From a broader perspective, the deepening of China-Europe EV cooperation is also a microcosm of the transformation of the global car industry. For decades, the division of labor in the global automotive sector remained relatively fixed, and China was long a latecomer playing catch-up. But in the wave of electrification and intelligence, China has built distinct advantages in batteries and intelligent driving, while Europe retains profound accumulated strengths in traditional areas. Cooperation is a two-way journey where each side brings its own strengths to jointly define new products. Recognizing these new signals of cooperation does not mean the road ahead is smooth. China-Europe EV cooperation still faces multiple challenges, from geopolitical noise to protectionism. Chinese automakers need to adapt to changing market trends in Europe. Europe, for its part, must let reason overcome prejudice, respect facts, and treat Chinese carmakers fairly in line with WTO rules. The Paris Motor Show this time may be witnessing the arrival of a new era of industrial collaboration: the automotive industries of China and Europe can make the cake bigger through open cooperation and forge a path that benefits industry, companies and consumers alike.

item.title: Will the Pinglu Canal widen ASEAN's trade deficit with China?: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 21:40:00
A vessel sails along the Pinglu Canal near the Madao hub. Photo: Courtesy of Pinglu Canal Group Editor's Note: Currently, China's economy is steadily advancing along the path of high-quality development, even as domestic and international circumstances become increasingly complex. Some Western media, due to misunderstanding or bias, have repeatedly questioned or even distorted China's economic development. Accordingly, the Global Times launches the "Q&A on China's Economy" column to publish opinion pieces to present facts and clarify perceptions. The Pinglu Canal has been operational since September 16. As the latest landmark project in China-ASEAN connectivity, the canal is a public good serving the wider region. However, since construction of the canal began, there have been noises in the West and certain ASEAN countries arguing that lower logistics costs could "flood" ASEAN markets with more Chinese goods, leading to trade "imbalance" between China and ASEAN and posing challenges for the development of local industries in Southeast Asia. Such concerns are based to some extent on the realities of regional trade and economic relations, but the logic behind them is overly simplistic. As is well known, China and ASEAN have remained each other's largest trading partners since 2020. Their industrial chains are deeply interconnected, with intermediate goods accounting for more than 60 percent of bilateral trade. At the same time, many ASEAN economies maintain large trade surpluses with the US and Europe while running trade deficits with China. Will the opening of the Pinglu Canal therefore widen ASEAN countries' trade deficits with China? Such a view is clearly one-sided, for two reasons. First, the current China-ASEAN trade pattern is determined by the regional division of labor in industrial and supply chains, not by the Pinglu Canal. The existing pattern of bilateral trade between China and ASEAN countries does not exist in isolation. It forms part of a triangular division of labor that has developed over time in the region and within global industrial chains. The opening of the canal will not change regional comparative advantages, nor will it create trade imbalances. One important fact should not be overlooked. Many ASEAN countries run trade surpluses with European and US markets, and these surpluses often rely on intermediate goods, components, machinery and equipment imported from China. ASEAN countries process and assemble raw materials and components imported from China, and then export the finished products to end markets in Europe and the US. As a result, some ASEAN countries run trade deficits with China while maintaining surpluses with Europe and the US. This stems from the current regional industrial division of labour. The logistical convenience brought by the canal helps ASEAN countries leverage regional supply chains to expand exports to third-party markets, generating mutually beneficial outcomes at the level of regional industrial chains. Second, as a public good for regional connectivity, the Pinglu Canal serves as a low-cost waterway that is open to market participants on both sides. It is not designed only to serve Chinese exporters. It can transport Chinese goods southward while also facilitating the movement of ASEAN agricultural products, minerals, forest products and components northward into China's vast inland consumer and production markets, and even onward to the broader Eurasian market. Currently, China's month-on-month year-over-year import growth rate has outpaced export growth for six consecutive months. China's catalytic role in regional and even global trade and the economy has become more pronounced. Against this backdrop, the Pinglu Canal will help China import more ASEAN products in the years ahead. The structure of industrial chains is not fixed. ASEAN countries are promoting industrial upgrading, and their capacity to export higher value-added products continues to grow. Amid elevated global energy prices, international freight rates and inflation, which have pushed up regional firms' costs and squeezed their profit margins, the low-cost transport route provided by the Pinglu Canal comes at an opportune moment, acting as a booster for ASEAN's manufacturing upgrade and facilitating easier access for locally manufactured products to China's inland markets. The opening of the Pinglu Canal will, in the long term, strengthen China-ASEAN trade and the resilience of regional industrial and supply chains. As ASEAN goods enter China's inland markets at lower logistics costs, ASEAN economies will also become more deeply integrated into industrial chains in China. ASEAN products, from agricultural goods such as fruit, rice, rubber and palm oil to resources such as bauxite, will be able to move beyond China's coastal markets and reach more deeply into its western inland regions. At the same time, the canal will make central and western China more open to ASEAN and can also promote the development and transformation of Chinese industries. The benefits of lower logistics costs brought by the Pinglu Canal can only be realized through joint efforts. Take the second ship lock on Xijin reservoir, regarded as a key gateway to the canal, as an example. It has handled a cumulative cargo volume of 70.8 million tons over the past three years. Realizing the canal's full potential requires China and ASEAN countries to jointly build and make good use of two-way logistics chains. As ASEAN goods gain lower-cost access to markets in Southwest China, enterprises, ports and logistics service providers along the route will all play important roles in shaping the emerging canal economy. In short, the so-called "one-way corridor" narrative is essentially a new variant of the "China squeeze" narrative. The mutually beneficial and win-win cooperation framework between China and ASEAN remains unchanged, and will stay so. Only by expanding the pie of regional cooperation can China, ASEAN and more countries secure larger slices for themselves. In this process, the Pinglu Canal will serve not only as a multiplier for the expansion and optimization of trade, but also as a catalyst for structural improvement.

item.title: Police probes man for doing pull-ups on beam at 1,500-y-o historic Hanging Temple in North China's Shanxi
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 21:05:00
Photo: Screenshot from CCTV A video of a man doing pull-ups on a beam at the 1,500-year-old Xuankong Temple, or Hanging Temple, in Datong, North China’s Shanxi Province, has gone viral recently, sparking public concerns about potential damage to the historic structure, China Central Television (CCTV) reported on Tuesday. The Hengshan Mountain Scenic Spot Management Center responded on Tuesday that the public security authorities have launched an investigation. According to a statement released by the management center, surveillance footage confirmed that the incident occurred on September 27 at the Mahavira Hall of the Hanging Temple. The individual involved uploaded the video to social media on October 11, triggering widespread public attention the next day. Upon learning of the incident, ancient architecture and heritage conservation experts were dispatched to conduct an on-site inspection. A professional inspection confirmed that the behavior had not caused any visible direct physical damage to the heritage structure at this stage. However, given that the temple is a cliff side structure built entirely of wood, with its beams, crossbeams and columns interlocked through traditional mortise-and-tenon structure to distribute loads, such hanging and pulling activities pose a potential risk of disturbing the structural balance of the wooden framework, creating a serious safety hazard, the statement said. First built during the Northern Wei Dynasty (386-534), the Hanging Temple is a nationally protected cultural heritage site and a rare cliff side wooden complex that house Buddhist, Taoist and Confucian shrines. Featuring an ingenious architectural design, the temple relies on crossbeams embedded in the cliff for structural support. Any abnormal force on its load-bearing components could disrupt its centuries-old structural balance and cause irreversible damage, the statement said. Therefore, stepping on, pulling, shaking or climbing on the temple’s structural components is strictly prohibited, as doing so violates both the scenic area management rules and legal protections for cultural heritage, the statement added. After the video sparked controversy, the police formally opened an investigation and said they will deal with the individual in accordance with the law, the statement said. Next, the scenic area will step up patrols in key areas, install more warning signs and strengthen on-site visitor management to better protect the cultural heritage site, according to the statement. item.title: Chinese courts sentence three Myanmar-based Wei family crime group members to death, demonstrating extraterritorial application of China's criminal law: expert
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 19:33:00
Photo: from People's Daily A Chinese court on Tuesday sentenced three members of the Myanmar-based Wei family criminal group to death in first-instance verdicts. Three others received life imprisonment, while 55 defendants were sentenced to prison terms ranging from three years and 3 months to 24 years. The Intermediate People's Court of Quanzhou and people's court of Nan'an, both in East China's Fujian Province, publicly announced their first-instance verdicts in a series of cases involving the Wei family criminal group on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, according to media reports. Wei Huairen, Chen Dawei and Liao Jingfang were sentenced to death, while Wei Qingtao, Kang Min and Xiong Hengxing were sentenced to life imprisonment. The other 55 defendants, including Su Hongxiang, Deng Zida and Chen Longjiang, received fixed-term prison sentences, along with additional penalties including fines, confiscation of property and deportation, as applicable. The courts found that since 2019, two criminal groups had exploited the Wei family's influence in the Kokang region of Myanmar to establish multiple criminal compounds in Laukkaing and provide armed protection for crime bosses operating there. The one group, led by Wei Huairen and Wei Qingsong, who is being handled in a separate case, included Chen Longjiang, a close subordinate, and armed force leaders Cha Guicheng and Yan Longdi, both of whom are also being handled in separate cases, among its key members. The other group, known as the Henry criminal group, was led by Wei Rong, Wei Qinghai, both of whom are being handled in separate cases, and Wei Qingtao. Its key members included family member Su Hongxiang and close subordinate Deng Zida. The groups relied on armed forces controlled by the Wei family to provide armed protection for multiple crime bosses who set up operations in the compounds. They independently or jointly with these operators committed a range of crimes, including telecom and online fraud, operating casinos, extortion, organizing prostitution, drug trafficking and organizing others to illegally cross national borders. The two groups were involved in gambling- and fraud-related funds totaling more than 12.2 billion yuan ($1.7 billion), according to the court findings. The Wei family criminal group also colluded with telecom fraud gangs operating in the compounds to kill people involved in fraud who refused to comply with their orders, resulting in the deaths of two Chinese citizens. In addition, Chen Dawei, a member of the Wei family, used armed forces under his control to kill people indiscriminately, causing the deaths of another two Chinese citizens. According to the documentary The Demise of Myanmar-Based Telecom Fraud, which offers a rare look into the brutal reality of Myanmar-based cyber-scam networks and China's crackdown on cross-border telecom fraud, Chen was asked how he felt when he pledged brotherhood with others and killed people in a ritual sacrifice to heaven. "Was there anything to feel? I felt nothing," Chen replied. The courts ruled that defendants including Wei Huairen and Wei Qingtao had organized, led or participated in criminal groups and committed crimes constituting seven offenses, including intentional homicide and fraud. The courts said the sentences were handed down in accordance with the law, taking into account the facts, nature and circumstances of each defendant's crimes, as well as the degree of harm they caused to society. Since 2023, China and Myanmar have carried out joint operations that led to the dismantling of four major criminal gangs in Myanmar's Kokang region, according to the Criminal Investigation Bureau of the Ministry of Public Security. From October last year to August this year, the number of telecom fraud cases in China declined year-on-year for 11 consecutive months. By the end of 2025, Chinese courts had concluded first-instance trials of more than 27,000 cases related to telecom fraud operations in northern Myanmar, with more than 41,000 repatriated suspects sentenced, according to China's Supreme People's Court, the Xinhua News Agency reported. Huo Zhengxin, a professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told the Global Times that the case falls under Article 8 of China's Criminal Law, which provides for the exercise of protective jurisdiction. The provision states that China's criminal law may apply when foreign nationals commit crimes outside China's territory against the Chinese state or its citizens, provided that the minimum penalty for the offense under Chinese law is a fixed-term prison sentence of at least three years, unless the act is not punishable under the law of the place where it was committed. "Protective jurisdiction is also a widely recognized basis for jurisdiction under international law," Huo said. As crime becomes increasingly transnational, offenses targeting Chinese citizens overseas have become a recurring concern. The Myanmar-based telecom fraud cases serve as a typical example of the extraterritorial application of China's criminal law. They demonstrate China's efforts to protect the personal safety and property rights of its citizens both at home and abroad, while delivering a strong deterrent to transnational organized crime, Huo said. The differentiated sentences handed down by the courts in accordance with China's criminal law also demonstrate that Chinese judicial authorities strictly apply the law and determine penalties based on the degree of culpability of each defendant, he said. Regarding deportation as an additional penalty in the verdicts, Huo noted that the punishment applies only to foreign nationals and stateless persons, and not to Chinese citizens or foreign nationals entitled to diplomatic immunity. Deportation can be imposed either as an independent punishment or as an additional penalty. When imposed as an additional penalty, deportation generally applies to defendants convicted of serious crimes and takes effect after they have completed their principal sentences or been released on parole, with the aim of preventing them from continuing to endanger public safety in China, Huo said.

item.title: China, South Korea reportedly restart joint patrols in Yellow Sea to curb illegal fishing, signaling improved maritime trust
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 17:07:00
A drone photo taken on Sept. 1, 2026 shows a fishing boat sailing out of a fishing port in Qingdao, East China's Shandong Province. The new fishing season in the Yellow Sea and Bohai Sea kicked off on Tuesday after a four-month summer fishing moratorium. Photo: Xinhua China and South Korea have reportedly resumed joint patrols in the provisional measures zone in the Yellow Sea after a four-year hiatus, with the move showing improved mutual trust and helping promote legal fishing and maritime cooperation, a Chinese expert said. South Korea's Embassy in China said that China and South Korea have been conducting joint patrols starting October 8 to crack down on illegal fishing and other violations in the relevant areas. The patrols, which will continue until October 17, mark the resumption of joint operations after a four-year suspension since 2022, Yonhap News reported on Monday. During the patrols, fisheries guidance and law enforcement officials from the two countries will board each other's vessels to exchange law enforcement methods and experience, while strengthening on-site coordination, according to the report. "Restarting joint law enforcement after four years, with law enforcement personnel from the two sides boarding each other's vessels, is an uncommon practice and reflects to some extent the level of mutual trust between China and South Korea," Lü Chao, a research fellow at the Liaoning Academy of Social Sciences, told the Global Times on Tuesday. The cooperation is beneficial to promoting legal fishing activities in the Yellow Sea, Lü said, noting that establishing joint law enforcement is "not an easy achievement" and represents a positive development after relations between the two countries improved. A South Korean embassy official in China was also quoted as saying that "one of the areas where cooperation results have emerged since the South Korea-China summit is the crackdown on illegal fishing." The official added that "through this joint patrol, the two countries will further strengthen cooperation and communication between their law enforcement agencies," according to the Yonhap News report. The joint patrols were carried out in accordance with an agreement reached by the two countries to enhance cooperation and eliminate illegal fishing activities. "The Chinese government has always called on Chinese fishermen to conduct fishing activities in accordance with legal rules," Lü said, adding that joint law enforcement could help reduce fishing-related disputes, ensure lawful fishing operations in relevant waters and promote a more institutionalized approach to curbing illegal fishing. Chinese authorities previously carried out a fishing moratorium law enforcement campaign from May 1 to September 16, launching intensive enforcement operations in multiple maritime areas, including waters near the eastern boundary line of the China-South Korea provisional measures zone. The campaign targeted serious violations such as organized illegal fishing, fishing vessels entering closed waters before the official opening of the fishing season, and illegal fishing activities involving high-powered speedboats. At the fourth China-South Korea meeting on maritime affairs dialogue and cooperation, held on September 21, the two sides agreed that maritime affairs are an important component of bilateral relations and pledged to continue working toward building the Yellow Sea into "a sea of peace, friendship and cooperation." The two sides agreed to make better use of maritime dialogue mechanisms, strengthen communication, properly manage differences, advance maritime boundary negotiations, and enhance practical cooperation in areas including defense, law enforcement, fisheries, scientific research, environmental protection, shipping, search and rescue, as well as ocean and polar affairs. Lü said that after South Korea's new administration adopted a more pragmatic approach, the two countries completed reciprocal visits within a few months, and the joint patrols were launched shortly after the maritime cooperation dialogue, which he described as a measure to enhance mutual trust between law enforcement agencies and promote bilateral relations. "Dialogue is necessary. It can help resolve relevant issues and also serve as a precautionary measure to prevent disputes from escalating into serious incidents," Lü added.

item.title: 16th Airshow China to showcase Navy equipment on large scale, multiple Air Force combat platforms to appear for first time
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-13 14:38:00
A J-35A stealth fighter jet of the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force flies over the Jinwan Airport in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, during the opening day of the Airshow China 2024 on November 12. Photo: Cui Meng/GT The Zhuhai city in South China's Guangdong Province is gearing up for the 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, also known as Airshow China, running from December 7 to 13. A press conference for the event was held in Beijing on Tuesday, briefing the public on the preparations and some highlights. The Global Times learned that, coinciding with the 30th anniversary of the airshow's launch, this year's edition will hit a new record in scale, expand international cooperation and extend its display dimensions. New equipment from both the Chinese People's Liberation Army (PLA) Air Force and Navy will appear together, presenting the military's new-quality combat capability in a systematic way. Experts said Airshow China is a "national window" onto China's self-developed aerospace and defense technologies, and an important platform for technological exchange, trade talks and dialogue on peace, carrying significance for advancing the aerospace industry and maintaining regional peace and stability. Air Force to debut multiple main combat equipment As China's only State Council-approved international aerospace exhibition, Airshow China is held every two years. Since 1996, it has been held 15 times, growing from a regional show into one of the world's top five aerospace and defense events. Zhang Hu, a member of the Standing Committee of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee, executive vice governor of Guangdong Province and provincial government spokesperson, said this year's show will display over 3,000 pieces of equipment, with first-time exhibits estimated at 10 percent. The main exhibition area will host over 170 aircraft, with both domestic and foreign aerobatic teams performing. The PLA Air Force's exhibits have long been a highlight. In 2024, the J-35A stealth fighter jet's first official appearance made international headlines. "The star of Airshow China, which showcases Beijing's civil and military aerospace sector every two years in the southern city of Zhuhai, is the new J-35A stealth fighter jet," AFP said in its 2024 coverage, when the J-35A made its debut. Gao Xiang, deputy director of the political work department of the PLA Air Force, said this year's exhibits will cover reconnaissance, early warning, air defense, support, airborne operations, unmanned applications, intelligent equipment and munitions, fully presenting the service's equipment renewal and evolving combat system. "The lineup includes both combat-tested main combat platforms and publicly displayed upgraded equipment and new-quality combat capabilities," Gao said. "Some have made breakthroughs in type or quantity; others have innovated in air-ground coordination and display methods. The share of new-quality combat forces has increased, and multiple main combat equipment will make their Airshow China debut." The displays will show the public the Air Force's improved combat readiness and modernization achievements. Maritime display zone opens A key feature is the "one show, three zones" layout: the main venue at the Zhuhai International Airshow Center, the Gaolan Port maritime equipment display zone and the Lianzhou unmanned equipment exhibiting zone, extending the display of active-duty equipment to the sea and forming an integrated air, space, sea and land display system. "This year's airshow expands into the maritime dimension for the first time, opening the Gaolan maritime equipment display zone and enabling a large-scale, concentrated showing of active-duty Navy equipment," Zhang said. Zhang Junshe, a Chinese military affairs expert, told the Global Times on Tuesday that the expansion extends the display from "sky" to "sea," achieving comprehensive air, land, sea and space defense coverage and making the show more three-dimensional. In 2024, the PLA Navy brought real equipment to the airshow for the first time, including the J-15T carrier-based fighter, Z-9F carrier-based anti-submarine helicopter and Y-8 anti-submarine patrol aircraft. Two years later, the Navy is returning with a major maritime lineup. The Wall Street Journal noted the J-15T's appearance in 2024, reporting that China's navy showcased a new variant of its J-15 fighter that can be launched off aircraft carriers using a catapult system - a capability that Beijing has added to its newest carrier. "The Navy's move from a first appearance in 2024 to a large-scale display of active-duty equipment in 2026 marks a qualitative shift from 'testing the waters' to 'gaining a solid foothold,'" Zhang Junshe said. The expert added that Gaolan Port's deep-water conditions will allow the public to board ships for close-up visits, upgrading the experience from "looking at models behind a fence" to "immersive tours of real vessels." "Through this international airshow, the Navy will show its resolve to strengthen sea power and focus on combat readiness, raising public awareness and influence of its equipment." The Lianzhou unmanned equipment exhibition zone will serve as a demonstration platform for drones and anti-drone systems, according to the conference. Dynamic anti-drone demonstrations will be a highlight, with companies showcasing multiple countermeasures and the latest developments in drone counter-technology. Several new drone models will also take part in flight demonstrations. International platform As a major international aerospace and defense event, the airshow will again serve as a platform for global exchange and cooperation. This year's edition is more international than ever. Delegations from Russia, the US, France and Germany have expanded their participation, while companies from Belt and Road partner countries such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Singapore are deeply involved. More than 170 aircraft have registered for the main display area, a new record. Zhang Junshe said that since 1996, nearly 50 countries and regions and over 1,000 companies have viewed China's aerospace innovation and the systematic debut of new Air Force and Navy equipment through this window. Hao Changfeng, spokesperson for China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation, told the Global Times the company has participated in the event since 1996. "Over 30 years, our exhibits have grown from a few scattered items to a full spectrum of missiles, rockets, satellites, spacecraft and equipment, extending into commercial space, the low-altitude economy and space digital intelligence," he said. "Behind this shift is China's aerospace journey from catching up to running alongside, and in some areas leading." An anonymous military commentator who has attended the airshow multiple times told the Global Times on Tuesday that the event allows domestic and foreign companies to deepen exchanges and grasp the latest trends in global aerospace technology. Ahead of this year's show, Chinese aviation equipment has seen a string of delivery and procurement developments overseas. In August, Uzbekistan's state television publicly showed J-10CE fighters bearing the country's insignia, with six aircraft visible. Bangladesh is advancing procurement talks, with draft agreements prepared. "The J-10CE, as an advanced fighter independently developed by China, has won multiple overseas orders, entered service in other countries and achieved combat results. It has always been a focal point at the show. How the J-10 series, especially the J-10C, will be displayed this year will be closely watched," the commentator said.
